explanations.explanation: Yes, friend, Dagon. The Philistines carry the ark into the temple of Dagon and set it beside his statue (1 Samuel 5:2). Dagon was the god of Ashdod. Remember that spot, because the next morning is something else.

Baal comes up elsewhere in the Bible, like in Judges 2:13, so I get why your mind went there. But this passage names a different god. The Philistines carry the ark into the temple of Dagon and set it beside his statue (1 Samuel 5:2). Dagon is the one whose morning is about to get rough.

Molech is a name you'll run into in Leviticus 18:21, friend, but not in this temple. The text says the Philistines carry the ark into the temple of Dagon (1 Samuel 5:2). They set it beside his statue, and that's where the trouble starts.

explanations.answer: Dagon fallen on his face before the ark
explanations.explanation: That's it. The people of Ashdod get up early and there is Dagon, fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD (1 Samuel 5:3). Nobody mentions a storm or an earthquake. I think those folks rubbed their eyes and checked twice, because I would have.

explanations.answer: The ark tipped over beside Dagon
explanations.explanation: Close, but the text doesn't say the ark tipped over. It says the people find Dagon fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD (1 Samuel 5:3). The statue is the one face-down, friend.

explanations.answer: The ark moved over to the doorway
explanations.explanation: No doorway trip for the ark here. The people of Ashdod find Dagon fallen on his face before the ark of the LORD (1 Samuel 5:3). The text doesn't move the ark anywhere, and the statue is the one in trouble. Doorways do come up in the next morning's story, but not for the ark.
Not quite, friend. They don't leave him lying there. The text says they took Dagon and returned him to his place (1 Samuel 5:3). They put him right back where he was.

Right, False. The text says they took Dagon and returned him to his place (1 Samuel 5:3). Nobody left him on the floor. I think they dusted him off and hoped nobody saw, like a guy who trips on the sidewalk and keeps walking.

explanations.answer: His head and hands are broken off
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. This time Dagon is on his face again, with his head and his hands broken off and lying on the threshold (1 Samuel 5:4). Only the torso remained. Standing him up one time was a nice try, and the second morning was a whole different story.
Not the feet, friend. The text says his head and his hands are broken off and lying on the threshold, and only the torso remains (1 Samuel 5:4). I'd say that's a lot more than a stubbed toe.

explanations.answer: His back is split in two
explanations.explanation: Nothing about his back, friend. The text says his head and his hands are broken off and lying on the threshold (1 Samuel 5:4). Only the torso remained. It's a rough morning, but it's a different kind of rough.

True. The text says that to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter his temple in Ashdod do not step on the threshold (1 Samuel 5:5). That's where the head and hands were found lying. I think they remember it every time they walk in, and they step high.

Not this time, friend. The text says that to this day, the priests of Dagon and all who enter the temple of Dagon in Ashdod do not step on the threshold (1 Samuel 5:5). The writer says it was still happening when this was written. Same threshold where Dagon's head and hands were lying (1 Samuel 5:4), and they still don't step on it.
That's right. The hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity, ravaging them and afflicting them with tumors (1 Samuel 5:6). Notice whose hand it is. The text names the LORD.

Not the priests, friend. The text says the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity (1 Samuel 5:6). The priests of Dagon show up earlier, as people who do not step on a threshold (1 Samuel 5:5). The heavy hand is the LORD's.

The rulers are coming up soon, but they're not the hand in this verse. It says the hand of the LORD was heavy on the people of Ashdod and its vicinity, afflicting them with tumors (1 Samuel 5:6). The rulers get called together a couple verses later, and they have a big question to answer.

explanations.answer: The ark must not stay with them
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. The men of Ashdod say, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay here with us…” (1 Samuel 5:7). They tie it to what they've seen: His hand is heavy upon them and upon their god Dagon. That's their decision.

explanations.answer: Dagon must move to a new temple
explanations.explanation: Not quite. Nobody votes to move Dagon. The men of Ashdod say, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay here with us…” (1 Samuel 5:7). It's the ark they want gone, friend.

explanations.answer: They must bring more gifts to Dagon
explanations.explanation: No extra gifts for Dagon in this story. The men of Ashdod say, “The ark of the God of Israel must not stay here with us…” (1 Samuel 5:7). They also say His hand is heavy upon them and upon their god Dagon, so they know whose hand it is.

That's the one. The rulers answer, “It must be moved to Gath…” and the people carry the ark away (1 Samuel 5:8). Gath is another Philistine city. I think everybody in Ashdod was thrilled to pass this one down the road.

Gaza is a Philistine city too (Joshua 13:3), but it's not the answer here. The rulers say, “It must be moved to Gath…” and the ark goes there (1 Samuel 5:8). Gath and Gaza start with the same letter, so I get the mix-up, friend.
Ashkelon isn't named in this passage. The rulers say, “It must be moved to Gath…” and the people carry the ark away (1 Samuel 5:8). Gath is the next stop on the ark's tour.

Not quite, friend. The text says the LORD's hand afflicted the men of the city, both young and old, with an outbreak of tumors (1 Samuel 5:9). It wasn't only the old men. Young and old are both named.

Right, False. The text says the LORD's hand was against Gath, afflicting the men of the city, both young and old, with an outbreak of tumors (1 Samuel 5:9). It also threw the city into great confusion. Young and old alike, so no age group got to say, "Not me."

explanations.answer: It was brought here to kill us
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. As the ark arrives, the Ekronites cry out, “They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!” (1 Samuel 5:10). The cry comes right as it arrives. I think Ekron was alarmed.

explanations.answer: It will bring our city great honor
explanations.explanation: Wouldn't that be nice? But that's not what they cry. The Ekronites say, “They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!” (1 Samuel 5:10). Nobody in Ekron is planning a welcome party, friend.

explanations.answer: It belongs beside our own god now
explanations.explanation: Not this time. The Ekronites cry out, “They have brought us the ark of the God of Israel in order to kill us and our people!” (1 Samuel 5:10). Their cry is about being killed, not about where the ark belongs. Nobody in it mentions setting the ark beside anything, friend.

True. The Ekronites call together all the rulers of the Philistines and say, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. It must return to its place…” (1 Samuel 5:11). They add that they want it gone so it will not kill them and their people. That's their whole request, friend.

This one is True, friend. The text says the Ekronites called together all the rulers of the Philistines and said, “Send away the ark of the God of Israel. It must return to its place…” (1 Samuel 5:11). They weren't asking where to move it next this time. They wanted it sent home.
Yes, friend. The outcry of the city went up to heaven (1 Samuel 5:12). Those who didn't die were afflicted with tumors. This is a heavy part of the story, and I think the city was in real misery.

Ashdod is where this story started, but it's not where the cry goes. The text says the outcry of the city went up to heaven (1 Samuel 5:12). Ekron was in real trouble, friend, and I think it showed in how loud they cried.

Shiloh isn't mentioned in this passage, friend. The text says the outcry of the city went up to heaven (1 Samuel 5:12). Those who didn't die were afflicted with tumors. This is a heavy part of the story.
